overview: This card follows communities represented by the atlas’s approximate 1492-1530 “taiwan” layer. It is not a kingdom, one ethnic group or the modern state. Austronesian-speaking peoples lived in distinct communities without an island-wide government. Archaeology supplies most evidence; the first surviving detailed eyewitness account dates to 1603 and covers a limited southern encounter.

periods.title: Regional Iron Age communities
periods.summary: Long before the atlas starts this card, communities across Taiwan combined stone, bone, pottery and metal technologies. Imported ceramics, glass and beads joined local production, but new tools did not create one island-wide state.

periods.title: The atlas window, not a reign
periods.summary: The two atlas snapshots color most of Taiwan’s main island as one record. Their changing outline and the absence of a documented unifying government make this a display interval for diverse communities, not a sovereign polity with a 1492 accession and 1530 fall.

periods.title: Growing maritime contact
periods.summary: After the atlas label disappears, seaborne contact became increasingly visible. Archaeological ceramics show uneven links with China and other routes; by the mid-sixteenth century Taiwan was becoming more prominent in East Asian maritime exchange without becoming one foreign-controlled colony.

periods.title: Eyewitness writing and competing visitors
periods.summary: Chen Di joined a 1603 Ming anti-pirate expedition and wrote the earliest surviving firsthand account of Indigenous societies on Taiwan. His hosts’ lives become unusually visible, but his brief outsider report cannot stand for every community or be pushed back unchanged to 1500.

periods.title: Colonial rule changes the stakes
periods.summary: The Dutch established a southern base in 1624 and the Spanish a northern one in 1626. Trade, migration, war and colonial institutions increasingly restricted Indigenous territory and autonomy; this later transition belongs chiefly to separate atlas cards.

items.text: The imported index gives “taiwan” an approximate 1492-1530 lifetime. Those dates match atlas snapshots, not a founding, coronation, conquest or collapse. The label is a modern geographic convenience for an island whose communities had their own names and identities.

The 1492 feature is one 138-vertex main-island polygon. Point tests place Taipei, Keelung, Tainan, Hualien, Taitung, Hengchun and Yushan inside, while Penghu, Green Island, Orchid Island and Kinmen are outside. A filled outline does not prove one government controlled every mountain and coast.

The 1500 feature shrinks to 29 vertices and drops tested points at Tamsui, Keelung, Hualien, Taitung and Hengchun while retaining Taipei, western cities and central mountains. No matching political event explains that odd shape. It is a geometry artifact, which is why the history below does not imitate it.

This record is also separate from “taiwanese-tribes” (1200-1279), “dutch-formosa” (1650-1715), “taiwan-1878” and “taiwan-1945.” The modern card begins in 1945. Atlas gaps and handoffs are filing choices, not times when people or the island vanished.

sections.title: Many peoples, villages and political arrangements

items.text: Taiwan held varied Indigenous societies rather than one “Taiwanese tribe.” Their languages belong to the Austronesian family, whose relatives stretch from Madagascar through Island Southeast Asia into the Pacific. Shared ancestry did not mean one language, ruler or custom.

Archaeology likewise warns against turning an island into one polity. Late prehistoric communities adopted foreign porcelain, beads and metals selectively, yet the evidence generally points to locally organized societies. Some areas were more hierarchical than others, and several later reports describe politics centered on individual villages.

Chen Di’s 1603 hosts lived in the southwest, likely among Siraya-speaking people. He wrote that islanders were “of diverse kinds” and described his hosts as having no officials or chiefs. That valuable observation is close in time, but it is one visitor’s twenty-one-day encounter, not an island census.

Communities were neither isolated nor frozen. The earliest records describe trade, intermarriage, warfare and alliances between settlements. Archaeology adds a longer view: imported objects circulated without erasing local pottery, tools, foodways or political choices.

sections.title: Iron, pottery and an island in exchange networks

items.text: Northern craftspeople at Shihsanhang smelted iron, while stone tools, bone tools and patterned pottery remained useful. “Iron Age” therefore does not mean everyone threw away older technologies. A household might value a sharp iron tool and still cook, store or serve food in hand-built pottery.

The Shihsanhang finds include bronze, glass, beads and gold or silver objects, evidence of exchange beyond one village. Its star object is a three-dimensional human-faced pottery jug, described by the museum as unique in Taiwan. Imagine a pot that appears to watch you eat dinner.

In the southwest, Niaosong-period sites preserve rice, Job’s tears and iron tools, along with evidence for both larger and smaller settlements. Later Siraya layers contain still more iron, traded stoneware and porcelain, worked antler and glass ornaments. The sequence shows change and continuity, not a sudden 1492 beginning.

Chinese ceramics reached parts of Taiwan between the tenth and sixteenth centuries, but the main Fuzhou-Ryukyu and Quanzhou-Luzon routes may often have skimmed its coasts. Trade was real and uneven. A porcelain sherd proves contact far better than it proves foreign political rule.

Ironworking itself was an achievement of patient heat control. Excavations at Heping Dao and other northern sites suggest small-scale production suited to household needs and exchange. The technology was locally adapted; archaeologists caution that slag and metal objects do not automatically equal factories, specialists or powerful kings.

Chen Di described courtship among his 1603 hosts in which a prospective husband joined the woman’s family and the woman decided how long courtship continued. He also saw women doing much agricultural work. These details illuminate one southwestern society near the period; they should not be made into rules for every family on the island.

Dinner varied by place and season. Northern Shihsanhang refuse included bones or shells from deer, boar, fish, birds and shellfish. Southwestern archaeological layers preserve rice and Job’s tears. Together they suggest mixed farming, gathering, fishing and hunting rather than one island-wide menu.

A slightly later description turns a deer hunt into teamwork: large groups surrounded exhausted animals, then meat was cut and sun-dried. Deerhide could become clothing, armor or bedding and was exchanged for imported goods. This early seventeenth-century evidence is a bridge, not permission to give every 1500 household the same blanket.

Late prehistoric house remains at northern Heping Dao include floors, pits and many postholes interpreted as domestic units. Posts tell us that people built homes; they do not reconstruct a universal floor plan. Roofs, sleeping arrangements and household size varied and often leave little trace.

Children are hardest to hear in these sources. Pots, farming, navigation, hunting and metalwork all required teaching and practice, so learning plainly happened. Archaeology cannot tell whether a lesson looked like imitation, storytelling, a special initiation or several of these. There is no evidence here for a 1500 classroom timetable.

Clothing also resists a single costume. A visitor in the 1620s described traded cloth and deerhide bedding in one southwestern setting, while archaeology preserves ornaments better than fibers. Humidity is rough on old fabric, so glass beads may survive after a child’s shirt has completely disappeared.

sections.title: Learning, speech and a careful writing sample

items.text: More than twenty Indigenous languages are documented for Taiwan; no one language was “Taiwanese” in 1500. Some western-plains languages were later lost or became dormant, while living communities and revitalizers carry many others forward.

No local inscription from this atlas slice is securely known in the sources used here. Chen Di said his 1603 hosts had no writing, but that observation concerns those hosts and his idea of writing. It does not mean they lacked history, law, memory, poetry or sophisticated oral knowledge.

A useful language sample is the scholarly reconstruction *zalan, “road,” in Proto-Austronesian. The asterisk means linguists reconstructed an ancestral spoken form; it is not a 1500 spelling found on a stone. Related forms across Taiwan and the Pacific help reveal a language family whose speakers traveled astonishing distances.

The near-period written sample is 東番記, Dōngfān jì, the title of Chen Di’s 1603 Classical Chinese “Record of Dongfan/Formosa.” It is an outsider’s title, not an Indigenous self-name. Modern scholarship also warns that translating Dongfan automatically as “Eastern Savages” can force a loaded meaning onto what Chen used as a place-name.

sections.title: Health, water, drains and the missing loo

items.text: A preliminary study examined 23 well-preserved adult skeletons from broadly dated Shihsanhang burials. Cavities, abscesses, tooth loss and major trauma were uncommon in that sample, while tooth-enamel and eye-socket changes recorded episodes of bodily stress. Twenty-three selected adults are clues, not a health report for an island.

Bones can record injury, nutrition or disease, but they rarely name the healer, remedy or caregiving ritual. The Shihsanhang authors called their work preliminary and found no clear infectious disease in their selected skeletons. That does not prove nobody became sick, or reveal which medicines communities used around 1500.

Archaeology sometimes finds water management: much earlier Beinan houses in eastern Taiwan had outdoor aisles, storage rooms and drainage ditches. Those drains are valuable evidence, but they predate this card by well over a millennium. They cannot be quietly promoted into 1500-era sewers.

The honest toilet answer is that the archaeological and near-period sources consulted here identify pottery, postholes, drains, food remains, burials, iron slag and beads, but no securely dated 1492-1530 latrine. Waste disposal certainly happened; its exact place and plumbing are unknown. Even historians must sometimes write “loo: evidence pending.”

Contact did not begin with Europeans. Ceramics and other objects show centuries of selective exchange, while merchants and fishers from nearby coasts visited without annexing the whole island. Archaeology helps restore Indigenous people as active choosers and adapters, not scenery waiting for an “Age of Discovery.”

By 1603, violent maritime competition touched local communities: Chen Di accompanied a Ming expedition against Japanese-associated pirates and met Indigenous hosts who offered deer meat and wine after the fighting. The encounter produced precious evidence, but also reminds us that writing often arrived attached to armed outsiders.

From the mid-sixteenth century Taiwan became more visible in maritime competition. The Dutch established a southern colony in 1624; Spaniards followed in the north in 1626. The museum presents both connection and disruption, asking whose viewpoint shapes stories of arrival.

People did not end in 1530. Communities and languages continued, then faced successive colonial and state powers. The separate modern card follows Taiwan from 1945. This ending is continuity through a database gap, followed by profound transformation.

ending.text: Nothing fell in 1530. The atlas record stops, while Taiwan’s diverse Indigenous communities continued. Later maritime trade and colonial rule transformed their lands and choices; their descendants, languages and cultural work remain part of Taiwan today.
